title: Green‐synthesized silver nanoparticles from Xanthium strumarium for efficient removal of methyl orange and methylene blue from aqueous systems
content:
Abstract

Sustainable nanomaterial synthesis and its application in wastewater remediation are of growing environmental significance. In this study, silver nanoparticles (AgNPs) were synthesized via a green plant-mediated route using Xanthium strumarium leaf extract (XSLE) as both a reducing and stabilizing agent. UV–visible spectroscopy confirmed nanoparticle formation through a surface plasmon resonance band at ~433 nm. X-ray diffraction revealed reflections corresponding to the (111), (200), (220), and (311) planes of face-centered cubic silver, with an average crystallite size of ~28 nm. Scanning electron microscopy analysis indicated aggregated nanoparticle clusters with irregular morphology, while energy-dispersive x-ray spectra confirmed elemental silver with minor phytochemical residues. Transmission electron microscopy images further verified particle morphology and size, and selected area electron diffraction patterns indicated polycrystallinity. The adsorption of methyl orange (MO, λ max = 464 nm) and methylene blue (MB, λ max = 664 nm) followed a pseudo-second-order kinetic model, suggesting chemisorption, and Langmuir isotherm fitting (R 2 > 0.995) yielded maximum adsorption capacities of 4.96 mg g−1 (MO) and 5.78 mg g−1 (MB). Enhanced dye removal is attributed to high surface area, electrostatic attraction, and π–π interactions mediated by surface-bound phytochemicals. These results demonstrate that biogenic AgNPs act as crystalline nanomaterials and efficient, eco-friendly adsorbents for sustainable wastewater treatment.
